question: to the Commission Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová (Renew), Krzysztof Brejza (PPE), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Hilde Vautmans (Renew), Estelle Ceulemans (S&D), Martin Hojsík (Renew), Marie Toussaint (Verts/ALE), Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE), Lynn Boylan (The Left), Sara Matthieu (Verts/ALE), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Robert Biedroń (S&D), Thomas Waitz (Verts/ALE), Leoluca Orlando (Verts/ALE), Raquel García Hermida-Van Der Walle (Renew), Damien Carême (The Left), Sebastian Everding (The Left), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Hannah Neumann (Verts/ALE), Brando Benifei (S&D), Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Markéta Gregorová (Verts/ALE), Birgit Sippel (S&D), Diana Riba i Giner (Verts/ALE), Nikolas Farantouris (S&D), Marco Tarquinio (S&D), Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left), Matjaž Nemec (S&D), Chloé Ridel (S&D) Subject:

As acknowledged by the Commission, EU funding instruments, including Horizon Europe and the European Defence Fund, have supported companies active in the cyber-surveillance sector, including those in the spyware technology sector, such as Intellexa, Cognyte and Paragon. The European Parliament’s Committee of Inquiry to investigate the use of Pegasus and equivalent surveillance spyware identified serious concerns regarding the misuse of spyware technologies against journalists, political actors and civil society representatives, raising important questions about compliance with EU values, the protection of fundamental rights and oversight mechanisms. The revised Financial Regulation1 introduced an additional Early Detection and Exclusion System (EDES) ground for exclusion concerning entities involved in activities contrary to EU values. The Commission also stated that grave professional misconduct and serious breaches of fundamental rights may justify exclusion from EU funding programmes. In this context: 1.
Has the Commission assessed whether entities operating in the cyber-surveillance sector, including those involved in spyware, may fall within the scope of the revised EDES provisions?

Does the Commission intend to develop specific guidance or risk-assessment criteria regarding access to EU funding for companies implicated in documented breaches of fundamental rights or violations of EU values?
Has EDES previously been applied in relation to entities operating in the dual-use or cyber-surveillance sectors, and if so, for what categories of cases?

Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2024/2509 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 September 2024 on the financial rules applicable to the general budget of the Union (OJ L, 2024/2509, 26.9.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/2509/oj). 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.8.2026) 1. The Commission considers that existing mechanisms provide sufficient legal tools to prevent EU funds from being awarded to entities that are involved in activities incompatible with EU values, provided that their involvement in such activities is substantiated by concrete, reliable, and admissible evidence and meets the legal requirements laid down in the Financial Regulation1, and notably the early detection and exclusion system (EDES)2 rules. Where such activities constitute grave professional misconduct under the ground of incitement to discrimination, violence or hatred, or any other activities contrary to EU values, such findings must result from a final judgment. In the absence of such a judgment, the ground of exclusion is applicable on a preliminary classification in law by the EDES Panel referred to in Article 145 of the Financial Regulation. In such cases and based on individualised assessments and following adversarial procedures, exclusion from EU funding is mandatory. 2. Breaches of fundamental rights or EU values are considered at different stages of the application for and implementation of EU financial support. The Commission’s data mining and risk-scoring tool Arachne+3 can support the Member States in risk assessment, but no specific risk indicators can currently assess breaches of fundamental rights or values. 3. The information on whether EDES had previously been applied in relation to entities operating in the dual-use or cyber-surveillance sectors is not available, as there is no existing list indicating the sector in which an entity that has been the subject of an EDES proceeding operates. Similarly, for reasons of confidentiality, the Commission is unable to provide information regarding ongoing Panel cases.
